passage:
Dear Diary,
There is a new girl in our class called Gurleen. She is the tallest in our class and she laughs all the time, and everybody likes her. I think she is the cleverest too, and she would never tell a lie. Today I chose her as my partner for the science project because of that. Then she told Miss that she had finished our chart, but she hadn't even started. I did it all. Miss praised her. I felt funny inside. Maybe she forgot. She is so nice, so she must have forgotten.
Kishore

qa.q: Who actually made the science chart?
qa.a: Kishore did it all, though Miss praised Gurleen.

qa.q: Why does Kishore decide Gurleen must have forgotten?
qa.a: Gurleen is tall, cheerful and liked, so Kishore feels sure she must also be honest, and the lie gets explained away to keep that glow.

qa.q: What could Kishore think about the next time choosing a partner?
qa.a: Kishore could think about what the classmate has actually done, like finishing work or keeping promises, rather than how cheerful or tall they are.

qa.q: How might Miss feel on learning who really made the chart?
qa.a: Miss would probably feel sorry about praising the wrong child and want to give Kishore the credit.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also clever and honest, and explaining away her lie.

passage: In the village school near Ujjain, Manoj was the tallest boy in Class 5, always smiling, the first to be picked for kabaddi. Dhruv thought he must also be the smartest and the most honest. When Manoj said he'd return Dhruv's geometry box after the weekend, Dhruv handed it over without a thought. On Monday Manoj said he had lost it. On Wednesday Dhruv saw the same box, with his initials scratched inside, in Manoj's bag. His stomach twisted. But when he told his mother, he added quickly, "Maybe it's a different box. Manoj is good." She looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Dhruv see in Manoj's bag on Wednesday?
qa.a: He saw the same geometry box, with his initials scratched inside.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv say "Maybe it's a different box"?
qa.a: Manoj's height, smile and kabaddi skill made Dhruv believe he must be honest too, so the evidence feels wrong and gets explained away.

qa.q: How could Dhruv's mother help him?
qa.a: She could gently point to the initials, help him see that being cheerful or good at kabaddi says nothing about keeping promises, and help him ask for the box back.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's mother feel looking at him for a long moment?
qa.a: She may feel protective and a bit worried, seeing her son doubt his own eyes to keep believing in a classmate.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful, popular classmate must be honest and explaining away clear evidence.

passage: On the first day of the new term in Lisbon, Paulo arrived: tall, sunburnt from summer, laughing at everything. By lunchtime Chidi had decided Paulo was the best at everything. "He'll be class captain," Chidi told his mother. "He's clever and he never lies, you can tell." In the pair maths quiz that afternoon, Chidi let Paulo decide every answer, even when Chidi thought differently. They got four out of ten. Two of the answers Chidi had wanted to write were right. "But Paulo looks so smart," Chidi said later, confused.

qa.q: What score did Chidi and Paulo get in the pair quiz?
qa.a: They got four out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Chidi let Paulo decide every answer?
qa.a: Paulo's height, tan and laughter made him seem clever in every way, so Chidi trusted him over his own thinking.

qa.q: What could Chidi try in the next pair quiz?
qa.a: He could say his own answer and check it with Paulo, since being cheerful doesn't mean being right in maths.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel on learning that Chidi trusted him over his own answers?
qa.a: Paulo might feel surprised and a bit uncomfortable, since he never claimed to be good at maths.

grounding: Shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful new classmate is also clever and honest, and trusting him over his own answers.

passage:
The school library had a new rule: each Class 4 pair would run the book-return box for a week and enter a quiz at the end. Himani wanted Pallavi as her partner before the teacher had even finished speaking. Pallavi was the tallest girl in class, and she laughed so easily that even the librarian smiled at her.
"She'll know all the quiz answers," Himani whispered to her friend. "And she'd never forget anything. She's too nice."
On Wednesday, Pallavi left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play. Three books slid out in the rain. In Friday's quiz, Pallavi guessed most answers with a big grin, and they came sixth.
Walking out, Himani looked at Pallavi, who was still laughing with everyone. "You're really fun," she said slowly. "But you're not so good at quizzes, na?"

qa.q: Where did Pallavi leave the return box on Wednesday?
qa.a: She left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play.

qa.q: Why did Himani feel so sure Pallavi would know every quiz answer?
qa.a: Pallavi was tall, cheerful and liked by everyone, so to Himani it felt natural that someone so nice must also be clever and careful.

qa.q: What could Himani try next time she chooses a partner for a task?
qa.a: She could ask herself what the task really needs, like remembering things or knowing answers, and look for who has shown that, not just who is the most fun.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about being chosen and then hearing Himani's last comment?
qa.a: Pallavi may have enjoyed being picked first, but the last comment might sting a little, or she might just laugh it off, since being fun was never a promise to be good at quizzes.

grounding: It shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate must also be clever and reliable, one pleasing trait spreading to everything.

passage:
I'm Disha, and on Tuesdays I collect my cousin Mehak from school in Bengaluru. She's eight. Lately every story on the walk home has been about a boy called Yohan: the tallest in her class, always laughing, the first one picked for every game.
"Yohan says the moon follows only our car," she told me. "He's always right."
Last week she showed me her maths homework. Two sums were crossed out. "Yohan told me the answers. He's the smartest." When I asked if she had checked them, she looked at me as if I'd said something rude.
I can't know for sure what goes on in her head. It seemed that because Yohan is tall and cheerful, she had decided he must also be clever and truthful about everything. On Friday she said, quite quietly, "Yohan got his own sums wrong too." She didn't sound angry, only puzzled.

qa.q: What did Yohan tell Mehak about the moon?
qa.a: Yohan says the moon follows only our car.

qa.q: What does Mehak's reaction to Disha's question about checking suggest she believed?
qa.a: Her look suggests she felt checking was unnecessary, even rude, because she trusted that a tall, cheerful boy like Yohan must be right about everything.

qa.q: How could Disha gently help Mehak without making fun of Yohan?
qa.a: Disha could ask Mehak what Yohan is really good at, like games, and then work the sums out together so Mehak sees that being fun and being right are different things.

qa.q: How does Disha see Mehak's admiration for Yohan?
qa.a: Disha finds it a little worrying but also understandable, and Disha is careful to admit not knowing for sure what Mehak is thinking, only what her words and looks suggested.

grounding: Told by an older cousin, it shows a child assuming a tall, cheerful classmate is also smart and honest in everything.
